entries.topic: Holy See vs Vatican City State: subjects, treaties, territory, size, population, extraterritorial properties

claims.text: Lateran Treaty Art. 2: Italy recognizes the sovereignty of the Holy See in the international field as inherent to its nature, in conformity with its tradition and the needs of its mission in the world.

Lateran Treaty Art. 3: Italy recognizes the Holy See's full ownership and exclusive and absolute sovereign power and jurisdiction over the Vatican, constituted as Vatican City; St Peter's Square remains normally open to the public and subject to Italian police powers, which stop at the foot of the Basilica steps unless invited; when the Holy See closes the Square, Italian authorities withdraw beyond Bernini's colonnade.

Lateran Treaty Arts. 13–16: Italy recognized the Holy See's ownership of the patriarchal basilicas of St John Lateran, St Mary Major and St Paul Outside the Walls, the palace at Castel Gandolfo (and Villa Barberini), properties on the Janiculum; Art. 15 gives the listed buildings plus the Datary, Cancelleria, Propaganda Fide (Piazza di Spagna), Holy Office and Vicariate the immunities international law grants to foreign diplomatic missions; Art. 16 bars expropriation and exempts them, and listed pontifical universities and colleges, from taxes.

Vatican City covers 0.44 km2 (44 hectares) and is partly surrounded by walls; Holy See offices also occupy extraterritorial properties in Rome with the immunities of foreign embassies under the Lateran Treaty.

Vatican City State has 673 citizens, 458 of whom live inside the walls (including 120 Swiss Guards); some 30% of citizens live outside, mostly on diplomatic posts; 66 cardinals are Vatican citizens (10 living inside); 882 residents of any citizenship as of 31 December 2024.

As of 9 January 2026, 184 states maintain diplomatic relations with the Holy See, plus the EU and the Sovereign Military Order of Malta; 93 embassy chancelleries accredited to the Holy See are based in Rome.

The Secretariat of State's list 'Agreements of the Holy See' (1929–2009) contains about 59 entries; only one is titled as an agreement of the Vatican City State: the Monetary Agreement with the European Union of 17 December 2009.

The 2009 monetary convention was signed in Brussels on 17 December 2009 by Archbishop André Dupuy, apostolic nuncio to the EU, for the Holy See acting as representative of Vatican City State, and by Commissioner Joaquín Almunia for the EU; in force 1 January 2010, replacing the convention of 29 December 2000.

Santa Maria di Galeria (Vatican Radio shortwave centre) is an extraterritorial area owned by the Holy See under 1951 agreements with Italy; an Italy–Holy See agreement on an agrivoltaic plant there was signed on 31 July 2025 (Gallagher; Ambassador Di Nitto) and the Italian Senate approved the ratification bill on 7 January 2026; it enters into force when both sides complete ratification.

entries.topic: Fundamental Law of Vatican City State 1929, 2000, 2023, 2026; papal powers; Pontifical Commission; Governorate

claims.text: Fundamental Law chronology: first published 7 June 1929 under Pius XI; replaced by John Paul II's law promulgated 26 November 2000, in force 22 February 2001; replaced by Francis's law of 13 May 2023, in force 7 June 2023; replaced by Leo XIV's law signed 31 July 2026, in force immediately.

2000 Fundamental Law Art. 1: the Pope, as sovereign of Vatican City State, holds 'la pienezza dei poteri legislativo, esecutivo e giudiziario'; during a vacancy these pass to the College of Cardinals, which may legislate only in urgent cases and for the vacancy only.

2000 Fundamental Law: Art. 2 reserves representation of the State in foreign relations and treaty-making to the Pope, exercised through the Secretariat of State; Art. 3 vests legislative power in a Commission of cardinals with a cardinal president appointed for five years, save matters the Pope reserves to himself; Art. 5 vests executive power in the Commission's President, assisted by a Secretary General and Vice Secretary General; Art. 15 judicial power exercised in the Pope's name; Art. 19 amnesty, pardon and clemency reserved to the Pope.

The 2023 Fundamental Law confirmed the Pope's 'fullness of legislative, executive and judicial powers', opened the Pontifical Commission to 'other members' besides cardinals (five-year terms), and required a three-year financial plan submitted to the Pope, with budgets guided by 'clarity, transparency and fairness'.

Leo XIV's motu proprio of 19 November 2025 repealed Art. 8(1) of the 2023 law that reserved the Commission presidency to cardinals; the 31 July 2026 law incorporates this: the Commission (Art. 8) is 'composed of Cardinals and other Members, including the President', appointed by the Pope for five years; the Governorate is directly accountable to the Pope; the Secretary General office may be entrusted to more than one person; Art. 22(1) refers the judiciary to the Law on the Judicial System.

Sister Raffaella Petrini, appointed by Francis in 2025 as first woman and first non-cardinal President of the Pontifical Commission and Governorate, holds both posts; CNA/CWR called the 2025 appointment 'legally irregular' until the law was changed. The 2026 law is the fourth constitution since 1929.

InfoVaticana: the 2026 law repeals the 2023 text in full, restates that the State exists to guarantee the Holy See's independence and sovereignty in line with the Lateran Pacts, and confirms the Commission exercises the legislative function and the Governorate the executive/administrative function.

entries.topic: Citizenship by office; Vatican courts and 2020s reforms; prisons and Italy under Lateran Art. 22

claims.text: Law No. CXXXI of 22 February 2011 (Benedict XVI) on citizenship, residence and access: citizens by right are cardinals resident in Vatican City or Rome, Holy See diplomats, and persons resident in the State by reason of office or service (incl. Swiss Guards); citizenship by administrative decision covers residents authorised for office, persons with papal authorisation to reside, and resident spouses and children of citizens. It replaced Law No. III of 7 June 1929.

Under the 2011 law citizenship is temporary except the Pope's: it lapses when the qualifying office ends, when domicile in the State ends, or for a cardinal when he moves outside Vatican City or Rome; family members lose it with the holder; children cease to be citizens at 18; a person who would become stateless acquires Italian citizenship (Lateran Treaty Art. 9).

Lateran Treaty Art. 21: cardinals resident in Rome, even outside Vatican City, are citizens of Vatican City for all purposes. Art. 9: all persons with stable residence in Vatican City are subject to the Holy See's sovereignty.

Vatican judicial bodies: a single judge (Giudice Unico), the Tribunal, the Court of Appeal and the Court of Cassation; investigation and prosecution by the Office of the Promoter of Justice; judges appointed by the Pope, subject only to the law; courts exercise power in the Pope's name; he may defer any case at any stage; the structure rests on Law CXIX (1987), LXVII (2008), CCCLI (2020, amended 2023) and the Fundamental Law.

Law CCCLI on the judicial system was signed by Francis on 13 March 2020 (announced 16 March), replacing Law CXIX of 1987: judges 'hierarchically dependent on the Supreme Pontiff'; drawn from university professors or noted jurists; curial officials barred; judicial bodies given autonomy of expenditure from the Governorate budget; the Promoter of Justice directs the judicial police section of the Gendarmerie.

Motu proprio of 30 April 2021: cardinals and bishops accused of crimes, previously tried only by the Court of Cassation (presided over by a cardinal), are now tried by the Tribunal like everyone else, with the Pope's prior consent ('the tribunal judges with the prior consent of the Supreme Pontiff'); the Court of Cassation consists of three cardinals and at least two associate judges.

Motu proprio published 12 April 2023 (in force 13 April): defined the Promoter of Justice's powers, allowed it to request dismissal in minor cases, abolished the requirement of a full-time magistrate on the Tribunal, and provided substitute judges and a deputy president.

Becciu proceedings status: in March 2026 the Court of Appeal declared the first-instance trial null and ordered a retrial, directing the Promoter of Justice to file the full investigation record; the appeal hearing was set for 29 October 2026; his lawyer Fabio Viglione said the defence is confident of 'the cardinal's complete innocence' (as of 19 September 2026).

Paolo Gabriele, the papal butler, was convicted of aggravated theft by a three-judge Vatican tribunal on 6 October 2012 and sentenced to 18 months; the Vatican said a sentence would be served in an Italian prison as it 'does not have any long-term prison facilities'; he was held in the Vatican police barracks and pardoned by Benedict XVI on 22 December 2012.

CNS (Sept 2012): the Vatican Promoter of Justice at the Court of Appeal, Giovanni Giacobbe, said Vatican criminal trials are 'extremely' rare; a prison sentence would be served in Italy under an Italian–Vatican agreement never before used; Mehmet Ali Ağca, who shot John Paul II in St Peter's Square in 1981, was handed to Italian police and convicted by an Italian court.

Lateran Treaty Art. 22: at the Holy See's request, or by delegation, Italy punishes in its territory crimes committed in Vatican City; if the offender has fled to Italy Italian law applies directly; the Holy See hands over persons who took refuge in Vatican City accused of acts committed in Italy that are crimes under both laws; same for the Art. 15 immune buildings.

entries.topic: Euro under the 2009 Monetary Agreement; tax exemptions; duty-free shops; utilities; health and hospitals; employees

claims.text: Monetary Agreement between the EU and Vatican City State, signed Brussels 17 December 2009, in force 1 January 2010 (Art. 13), repealing the agreement of 29 December 2000 (Art. 14). Art. 3(1): annual coin ceiling = fixed part (EUR 2,300,000 in 2010, revisable yearly for Italian HICP and the collector market) + variable part (Italy's average per-capita coin issuance times the Vatican population); Art. 3(2): extra commemorative/collector coins in years of sede vacante, offset against adjacent years.

2009 Monetary Agreement Art. 6(4): at least 51% of coins issued each year must enter circulation at face value; Art. 8: the Vatican must adopt measures implementing EU legal acts listed in the Annex on euro notes and coins, money laundering, fraud and counterfeiting of cash and non-cash means of payment, medals and tokens, and statistical reporting, updated annually by the Commission; Art. 11: Joint Committee of Vatican and EU (Commission, Italy, ECB) delegations deciding unanimously.

The EUR-Lex summary of the microstates' monetary agreements gives the Vatican a maximum annual coin issue of EUR 1 million (contrast: the agreement text's fixed part of EUR 2.3m from 2010) and states the three microstates may not issue euro banknotes.

Lateran Treaty Art. 17: salaries and other payments by the Holy See, the central entities of the Church and entities managed by the Holy See to dignitaries, employees and salaried staff are exempt in Italian territory from any tax from 1 January 1929. Art. 20: goods destined for Vatican City or Holy See institutions enter through any Italian border point or port with full exemption from customs and local duties. Art. 6: Italy to secure water supply, build a railway station and link Vatican telegraph, telephone, radio and postal services with other states, at its own cost within a year.

AP (Nov 2017): the Vatican stopped selling cigarettes to employees at its duty-free shop and supermarket, forgoing an estimated EUR 10 million a year; access requires a 'commercial card' (employees, retirees, residents, accredited diplomats, religious congregations); an Ernst & Young audit in 2013 found 41,000 cards in use against about 5,000 employees; purchases avoid Italy's 22% VAT; tax-free petrol was the largest source of such revenue per the 2015 book Avarice.

Il Post (8 May 2025): nearly 5,000 people work in Vatican City (about 2,000 in the Curia, the rest for the State); salaries are untaxed under the 1929 Pacts and broadly aligned with Italian pay; no VAT on goods sold in the Vatican; the Annona supermarket closed on 13 January 2025 for renovation and a five-year concession to an outside chain; employees' Fondo assistenza sanitaria (FAS) is funded by payroll contributions and gives serious cases priority access to Bambino Gesù and Gemelli hospitals; increments frozen 2021–23; the staff contract unchanged since 2008; hiring limited to one per three retirements.

Bambino Gesù Hospital, founded 1869 by Duchess Arabella Salviati, donated to the Holy See in 1924; extraterritorial area administered by the Holy See; part of Rome's National Health Service network; recognized as a research hospital (IRCCS) in 1985; 607 beds.

On 8 February 2024 Cardinal Parolin and Undersecretary Alfredo Mantovano signed a non-binding Declaration of Intent to build a new Bambino Gesù site at the former Forlanini hospital: the Holy See to acquire the area from Lazio, INAIL to build and lease, and an agreement extending Lateran Treaty Arts. 15–16 immunities to the new premises.

On 3 December 2025 the Chamber's budget committee approved an amendment to the 'decreto Economia' providing a State–Lazio property swap (Policlinico Umberto I to Lazio; Forlanini to the State) so the Forlanini area can pass to the Holy See for the new Bambino Gesù.

Francis's motu proprio Fratello Sole (21 June 2024) set the goal of 'the complete energy self-sufficiency of the Vatican City State' through an agrivoltaic plant at Santa Maria di Galeria; Leo XIV's chirograph of 1 June 2026 created the Fratello Sole Foundation to build and run it; the plant is still planned.

claims.text: Audit reconciliation: the Court of Appeal's ruling of 17 March 2026 was a partial mistrial ('relative nullity'); it ordered hearings renewed before the appeal court and the full file deposited, not a fresh first-instance trial; per Vatican News/ANSA the first-instance judgment keeps effect for now; AP described the indictment as nullified. The Unione Sarda/ANSA summary of 19 September 2026 ('declared the first-instance trial null and ordered a retrial') is a simplification; Part Four follows vt10's wording. Becciu indicted 3 July 2021, after the 30 April 2021 motu proprio.
Law Library of Congress (2012) gave Vatican City a population of about 800, of whom only about 450 residents held Vatican citizenship.
